deep.reconstruction:
This page is introductory and contains no mathematics. It finishes §2 and gives §§3-5 of Euler's attempt at a theory of pipe-flow losses.

§2 (end): The ideal-fluid theory says water fed to a fountain should rise almost to its source height. When it does not, this does not refute the theory; it shows that some obstacles were left out of the model.

§3: The loss of motion is attributed to friction ('attritus') of the water against the pipe walls. The argument is an analogy with solids sliding on polished planes. From this Euler infers qualitatively that the retardation must grow with the distance travelled in the pipe and with the narrowness of the pipe. In modern terms this is head loss increasing with L and with 1/D, the qualitative content of the later Darcy-Weisbach relation h_f ∝ (L/D)·v²/2g.

§4: Euler says many authors ascribe the loss to friction, but none, to his knowledge, has determined or even tried to investigate its laws. He announces he will try, since this is essential for applying theory to practice.

§5 (begins, continues on the next page): The smallest fluid particles may be treated as solids. Hence particles moving along the walls feel friction obeying the same laws as for solids, only much smaller because of their 'lubricity'.

The following pages (§§6-7) turn this into a Coulomb-type law. Wall friction on each fluid element is a fixed ratio (to be fitted experimentally, possibly material-dependent) of the force pressing the element against the wall, i.e. of the wall pressure. This is the programme the page sets up.
errors: Physically, the premise that fluid wall resistance behaves like dry Coulomb friction (proportional to normal force, independent of contact area and speed) is mistaken. The pressure-proportional law built on it in §§6-7 is the known flaw of E260. It does not predict the observed velocity dependence of losses, and real losses do not depend on the absolute pressure level. This page only states the analogy; the incorrect law is formulated on the next page.

The historical claim in §4 that no one had attempted to determine the laws of fluid friction is overstated. Newton (Principia, Book II, Sect. IX) posited resistance from 'lack of lubricity' proportional to relative velocity. Couplet (1732) had made pipe-loss experiments on the Versailles water supply. Euler's 'quantum mihi quidem constat' hedges the claim.

ideas.what: Attribution of head loss in long, narrow pipes to wall friction, with loss increasing with pipe length and decreasing diameter
ideas.modern_name: frictional head loss in pipe flow (qualitative L/D dependence; later Darcy-Weisbach / Prony / Chézy)
ideas.usually_credited_to: qualitatively ancient/practical knowledge; quantitative laws to Chézy (1770s), Prony, Darcy (1857), Weisbach (1845)
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6, 1761); see also Euler's hydraulic papers on fountains and pipes (e.g. E332 on water conduction)

ideas.what: Treating fluid particles as small solids subject to Coulomb-type sliding friction against walls
ideas.modern_name: dry-friction (Amontons-Coulomb) analogy for wall shear; precursor of a wall-friction closure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E260) for the fluid application; Amontons (1699) for the solid law
ideas.where_published: E260 §§5-7; discussed in Truesdell's editorial introductions to Opera Omnia ser. II, vols. 12-13 (unsure of exact location)

ideas.what: Methodological stance: discrepancies between theory and experiment indicate neglected forces, not false principles; an empirical friction coefficient is left indefinite to be fitted

deep.surprise_reason: This is a purely motivational page with no mathematics. Its ideas (wall friction as the cause of pipe losses, loss growing with length and narrowness) were standard. E260's Coulomb-type fluid-friction hypothesis is known and discussed in the history of hydraulics. Nothing here appears absent from the literature.
